subtitle: Same coin, three completely different battlefields. Pick the wrong one and you're playing a game you didn't sign up for.

blocks.content:
Most retail crypto traders don't actually know what kind of contract they're trading. They open Binance, buy BTC, then lose 20% in a month and assume "crypto is risky" — when in reality they were on perpetual futures with 5x leverage and didn't realize the liquidation price was 19% away.

Before anything else — risk management, indicators, candle patterns — you need to know what you're actually trading. Three flavors, very different rules:

rows: Fixed date (e.g. last Friday of quarter)
Yes — every 8h, longs pay shorts or vice versa

blocks.content:
You buy BTC. You own BTC. Price doubles, you doubled. Price drops 90%, you have 10% left. No leverage, no liquidation, no funding. You can wait 5 years for your bag to recover.

This is what "holding crypto" means in the strict sense. Good for long-term conviction plays. Bad for short-term opportunities (you can't short, and your gains are 1:1 with price).

blocks.title: Why retail isn't on spot
blocks.content: Most retail "crypto trading" looks like spot trading on the surface ("I bought BTC at 60k") but is usually perpetual futures with default 5-10x leverage. The exchange's UI doesn't always make this loud. Always check the badge: USDT-M Futures or Spot.

Contracts that expire on a specific date. "BTCUSD-1228" is a contract that settles on Dec 28. Common at CME and on offshore exchanges as "quarterly" contracts. The price often trades at a premium or discount to spot ("contango" / "backwardation"), which closes as expiry approaches.

Almost no retail trader uses these. They exist for institutions hedging — a miner can sell quarterly futures to lock in a price for the BTC they'll produce.

This is where 95% of crypto leverage activity lives. Same idea as a future, but it never expires. So how does the price stay anchored to spot? Funding rates.

Every 8 hours, if perp price is above spot, longs pay shorts a small fee (e.g. 0.01% of position). If perp is below spot, shorts pay longs. This continuous payment forces the prices to converge. It's elegant — and it's also a hidden cost most traders ignore.

blocks.title: Funding eats small wins
blocks.content: A trade held 3 days through three funding payments at 0.01% each = 0.03% in funding. On a 5x leveraged position that's 0.15% of your margin gone before any price move. If funding spikes to 0.1% (common during euphoric runs), you can pay 0.9% of margin per day just to hold.
How to tell which you're on

Open your exchange. Look for these cues:

  • Spot: tab says "Spot" or "Convert". No leverage selector. Order book shows actual BTC quantities. You can withdraw the BTC.
  • Futures / Perp: tab says "USDT-M Futures", "COIN-M Futures", "Perpetual", or you see a leverage selector (1x, 2x, 5x, 10x, 25x, 50x, 100x). Order quantities are denominated in contracts or USDT.
  • Test: try to set the leverage to 1x. If you can't change it, you're on spot. If you can, you're on a leveraged product.

blocks.title: Take this with you
blocks.content:
For the rest of this course, when we say "trade" we mean perpetual futures unless noted. That's where the journal lives, where the auto-trader runs, and where you'll spend 95% of your screen time.

Now go look at your exchange right now and confirm which market your wallet currently has open. Don't trust your memory.
